name: Computer science
question: What does computer science establish about this subject, divided by the property asserted of a computation?
scqa_question: By what single dimension can every claim about a computation be placed once, with the theorems left in MA?
look_for: CS.O.A1 Correctness
CS.O.A2 Cost
CS.O.A3 Coordination
CS.O.A4 Learning
CS.O.A5 Protection
rules_of_thumb: Premature optimisation is the root of all evil
"make it work, make it right, make it fast"
collisions: Place by the property claimed: correctness, cost, coordination, learning or protection.
A theorem is MA, even when computer scientists prove it. Complexity theorems sit in MA.B.C3; CS cites "uses MA.B.C3".
A program delivered to a customer's specification is EN (EN.B.C5); whether the program is correct is CS.
A claim about users' minds is MS; the interface's measured effect is CS.B.C8.
A claim about the record, the catalogue or retrieval as such is IS; the algorithm's cost is CS.
A claim about language is LN; a system that processes it is CS.O.A4.4.
The legal duty on data is LA; the technical privacy guarantee is CS.O.A5.3.
A claim mixing two properties goes to the one its warrant establishes.
computability and complexity theorems → MA.O.A1, MA.B.C3
the record and its retrieval as information → IS
ethics of AI as argument → PL
open: P vs NP (owned by MA.B.C3, cited); AI alignment methods (A4.5).
software engineering in EN vs CS (alternative: CS.O.A1); HCI as a CS bridge vs an MS cell.

name: Correctness
question: What can be claimed about correctness, and how?
look_for: Semantics of languages — operational, denotational and axiomatic semantics. Lambda calculus and Turing machines are equivalent in power (the theorem is MA.O.A1).
Specification and verification — Hoare logic proves partial correctness; total correctness also needs termination. Model checking decides temporal properties of finite-state models.
Types — well-typed programs do not go wrong (progress and preservation), for languages whose type system is proved sound.
Testing — testing can show the presence of bugs, never their absence (Dijkstra), for any input space too large to exhaust.
Limits of correctness — Rice's theorem: every non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable, for Turing-complete languages. Uses MA.O.A1.
breaks: specification wrong, unsound tool, unmodelled environment
open: software engineering in EN vs CS (alternative: CS.O.A1); HCI as a CS bridge vs an MS cell.

name: Cost
question: Which costs can be bounded, and by what?
look_for: Algorithms — each algorithm has a stated cost on a stated model. Comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case (a decision-tree lower bound, uses MA.B.C3).
Data structures — amortised costs, e.g. union–find with path compression and union by rank runs in O(α(n)) per operation.
Complexity classes — P, NP, PSPACE. Whether P = NP is OPEN and owned by MA.B.C3; CS uses it.
Machines and architecture — memory hierarchy, pipelines, parallel speed-up. Amdahl's law bounds speed-up by 1/((1−p) + p/s) for a fixed workload whose fraction p is parallelisable by a factor s.
Physical limits of hardware — Moore's law is an empirical trend, now slowing; it is not a law. Transistor physics is PH.
breaks: model mismatch with hardware, unrepresentative input

name: Coordination
question: What can and cannot be coordinated?
look_for: Concurrency — races, deadlock, linearisability.

Distributed agreement — FLP (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985): no deterministic protocol guarantees consensus in an asynchronous system if even one process may crash. This is a proved theorem, not an open problem. Byzantine agreement need
Consistency under partition — CAP (Gilbert and Lynch, 2002 proof): during a network partition, a system cannot provide both linearisable consistency and availability.
Networks — protocols, routing, congestion control.
Data systems — databases, transactions (ACID), query optimisation. Information retrieval as a claim about records is IS.
breaks: failure model differs from assumed one

name: Learning
question: What can such systems learn, and how well?
look_for: Learning theory — a binary concept class is PAC-learnable if and only if its VC dimension is finite (uses MA.O.A5). No-free-lunch: averaged uniformly over all objective functions, every optimiser performs equally.

Models and training — neural networks; universal approximation holds for one-hidden-layer networks with a non-polynomial activation, approximating continuous functions on compact sets to any accuracy. It says nothing about learnability. Emp
Reasoning and planning — search, logic programming, planning. Many planning problems are PSPACE-complete (uses MA.B.C3).
Perception and language processing — vision, speech, NLP. Claims about language itself are LN.
Alignment and evaluation of AI systems — whether a trained system pursues its intended objective. Methods are immature; much is OPEN.
breaks: data leakage, benchmark overfitting, distribution shift
collisions: A claim about language is LN; a system that processes it is CS.O.A4.4.

name: Protection
question: What can be protected, from whom, and on what assumptions?
look_for: Cryptography in use — protocols are secure relative to stated hardness assumptions (e.g. factoring). Security proofs are MA; the deployed protocol is CS.
Systems security — access control, memory safety, attack surfaces.
Privacy — differential privacy bounds how much one record changes an output distribution, by a stated ε.
Quantum threats — Shor's algorithm factors in polynomial time on a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Uses MA.B.C3 and PH.O.A2.
breaks: broken assumption, side channel, implementation flaw
collisions: The legal duty on data is LA; the technical privacy guarantee is CS.O.A5.3.
